Hello!
DefaultSettings.6_S6_L001_R1_001_val_1_bismark_bt2_pe.bismark.cov <https://msuclanac-my.sharepoint.com/:u:/g/personal/lwgent_uclan_ac_uk/Ef5irkBWkHBCmajI0zvcCVsBPKyg_V8xcxWf3l1gSSEU9A>

I'm still quite new at looking at sequencing data, and I'm currently just 'practicing' lets say with a pilot sample from a project I'm on with the methylKit package; so I'm not sure if I've read incorrectly but I may have caused a blunder for myself.

I initially tried it out what I believe is the standard or a standard way of doing it with the .cov file from bismark_methylation_extractors outputs? Directly with readMeth:

file.list <- list(  "DefaultSettings.6_S6_L001_R1_001_val_1_bismark_bt2_pe.bismark.cov")

myobj <- methRead(file.list,
sample.id <http://sample.id>=list("TestSample"),
pipeline = "bismarkCoverage",
assembly="hg38",
mincov = 10,
treatment = 1,
context = "CpG")

^^So lets put this aside for now.^^

I secondly instead just tried out the package with my BAM file with the aim of obtaining methylation rates for each of the positions with the processBismarkAln() function as I found a thread online that suggested it, like so:
'my.methRaw = processBismarkAln(location = "/Users/lukeg/OneDrive - UCLan/miSeq/BAM/DefaultSettings.6_S6_L001_R1_001_val_1_bismark_bt2_pe.sorted.bam.bam",
sample.id <http://sample.id> = "test1",
assembly = "hg38",
read.context = "CpG",
save.folder = getwd())'

This created 'test1_CpG.txt' which then I used methRead like so:
file.list=list("/Users/lukeg/OneDrive - UCLan/miSeq/BAM/m.gz")

myobj2=methylKit::methRead(file.list[[1]],
sample.id <http://sample.id>="test1",
assembly="hg38",
treatment=c(1),
context="CpG",
mincov = 10)

So I have two 'myobj' that were created differently, one via the .cov file and the other from the BAM after processBismarkAln. Seems both are the correct objects for the downstream steps, except they both have a different number of ranges, and the ranges of the same chromosome positions have different values when I create granges objects out of them with the worked out meth percentage values (I couldn't do it the standard way as the unite function to create the actual meth object instead of methraw is for if there are multiple samples in the BAM file).

This is an example of how I did it with the my.obj objects, I did the exact same thing with both:

myobj.filt <- filterByCoverage(myobj,
lo.count=10,
lo.perc=NULL,
hi.count=NULL,
hi.perc=99.9)

myobj.filt.norm <- normalizeCoverage(myobj.filt, method = "median")getCoverageStats(myobj.filt.norm[[1]],
plot=TRUE,both.strands=FALSE)

my.gr <http://my.gr> <- as(myobj.filt.norm[[1]],"GRanges")
my.gr <http://my.gr>
my.gr_df <- as.data.frame(my.gr <http://my.gr>)
my.gr_df$MethPerc <- (my.gr_df$numCs/(my.gr_df$numCs + my.gr_df$numTs))
my.gr_methperc <- FusionExpressionPlot::grAddColumn(my.gr <http://my.gr>, "MethPerc", my.gr_df$MethPerc)

library(annotatr)# Get premade CpG annotationsbuiltin_annotations()

hg38_cpgs_annotations <- build_annotations(genome = 'hg38', annotations = "hg38_cpgs")

my.gr_annotated <- annotate_regions(  regions = my.gr_methperc,  annotations = hg38_cpgs_annotations,  ignore.strand = TRUE)

my.gr_annotated

my.gr_annotated_df <- data.frame(my.gr_annotated)

Apologies if this is nonsensical, both scripts I used are attached. The main issue is, the differences between the granges objects at the same range and understanding why one created more strands than the other. For example, in my.obj, chr1 125178955  differs in its numCs and numTs than in my.obj2.

I'm happy to answer any questions.

Best,

Hi
I have been having a frustrating time trying to use methylkit on whole genome data.
I have a number of samples with relatively low coverage and others with great coverage. The samples with low coverage (and fewer sites, usually < 20 Mil) have no problems.
When I try to run the high coverage/high site count data (40 Mil and above, largest is 77 Mil) I get segmentation faults.
I have tried subsetting the data with awk to be sure smaller subsets of the data do work... they do.
It doesn't seem that there isn't anything wrong with the data or the file.
Is there an upper limit to the amount of sites that methylkit can handle?

messages.subject: Re: Is there an upper limit to the number of sites?
messages.subject_clean: Is there an upper limit to the number of sites?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ryan,

The available memory will define the upper limit of samples and sites.

You may be able to use tabix-based objects to circumvent this problem as the objects will be written to disk and only relevant chunks will be loaded into memory (see https://www.bioconductor.org/packages/devel/bioc/vignettes/methylKit/inst/doc/methylKit.html#22_Reading_the_methylation_call_files_and_store_them_as_flat_file_database
).

The counts per site should not be a problem, but samples with up to 40M sites (probably from non-CpG sites?)  might quickly fill up your available memory. I guess tabix files could help here.

Another option would be to process the samples in chromosome batches, which should also lower your memory burden.

Best,
Alex

Hello

In the process of trying to deal with big datasets that produce seg fault errors, I have resorted to splitting the *cov.gz by chromosomes.
I then process all individuals for one chromosome at a time.
This can get me up to the stage of uniting the samples (and greatly reducing the amount of sites by getting rid of sites that don't overlap between samples and sites with low variance).

Now I would like to concatenate the individual chromosomes so I can run a PCA  on the entire dataset (either through MethylKit or with custom code).

Is there a recommended way to concatenate data for the same individual within methylKit?

I know I could just paste the txt.bgz files for each individual together through the command line but I wanted to be sure there was not some caveats on doing this.

messages.subject: Re: methRead() multiple cores
messages.body_plain:
Hi Hélène,

As Ryan pointed out, parLapply can be used for this, but you should be aware that this increases the amount of available memory required.

The way I usually do this is via mclapply (also from the parallel package). This works only on Linux and Mac, for Windows you may have to use parLapply.

Please check out this example code:

```
library("methylKit")
library(parallel)

file.list=list(
  system.file("extdata", "test1.myCpG.txt", package = "methylKit"),
  system.file("extdata", "test2.myCpG.txt", package = "methylKit"),
  system.file("extdata", "control1.myCpG.txt", package = "methylKit"),
  system.file("extdata", "control2.myCpG.txt", package = "methylKit")
)

sample.ids=list("test1","test2","ctrl1","ctrl2")

treatment = c(1,1, 0,0)

res = methylRawList(
  treatment = treatment,
  mcmapply(
    FUN = methRead,
    file.list,
    sample.ids,
    assembly = "hg18",
    SIMPLIFY = FALSE,
    mc.cores = 3
  )
)

resDB = methylRawListDB(
  treatment = treatment,
  mcmapply(
    FUN = methRead,
    file.list,
    sample.ids,
    assembly = "hg18",
    dbtype = "tabix",
    SIMPLIFY = FALSE,
    mc.cores = 3
  )
)
```

Best,
Alex

Alex

messages.body_plain:
Hi Luke,

Sorry for the late reply, but I finally checked your scripts and files.

Concerning your questions, for one I have a rather clear answer, but the other requires some debugging.

First, the difference in strand usage that you observed between the different objects stems from a difference in the file formats: The Bismark coverage files do not contain strand information (see http://felixkrueger.github.io/Bismark/bismark/methylation_extraction/#optional-bedgraph-output), while the file generated by processBismarkAln does contain both strands.

However, this does not explain the difference in coverage thus I need to do some more debugging here.
I tested locally with some test files and there I did get similar results for cov/bam files (except strand), thus there might be some other things here that could cause differences, like low mapping quality of reads (>20 for processBismarkAln).

To do some more testing, it would be great if you could send me the bam file that you used, plus the bismark processing commands.

Best,
Alex
